description:
HostClaim takes one machine for your use. What it does to the machine:

- Creating it with spec.os proposes installing that TalosNode. Once the install is approved, the disk picked by the TalosNode's installDiskSelector is erased and overwritten.
- Deleting it releases the machine. If the operator installed the machine, it is shut down: a graceful shutdown first, then forced off after 5 minutes (the manager's --release-shutdown-timeout). If the machine runs a node, the shutdown waits for approval unless spec.provisioning.approval is Automatic. A machine the claim never installed is left running.
- Without spec.os the claim only reserves the machine; nothing is done to it.

Each proposed step is a HostOperation; with approval Required (the default) it waits until you run pk-metal approve <namespace>/<operation>. To stop all proposals for a claim, set the metal.pk.io/hold annotation on it. After a finished install, status.handOff records which machine runs which node; the operator does not install it again.

A claim binds exactly one Host, and only one claim can hold a Host. Keep claims in git, so that taking a machine is a reviewed change.

fields.name: spec
fields.description:
HostClaimSpec says which machine you want and what it should run. You pick the machine by its Asset, because you know the Asset name before the operator has found the machine and named its Host.

A claim that you point at another machine (pk-metal replace) moves. The operator first releases the machine that the claim holds, as a deletion of the claim does: the node leaves the cluster, and the machine is reset or marked as not wiped. This needs approval where it turns a node off. Only then does the operator bind the new machine, so two machines never run the same node. Only an admin can do this (config/policy/hostclaim-provisioning.yaml). It moves the config of a node to another machine, and on a control plane also the keys of the cluster.

fields.name: assetRef
fields.description: AssetRef names the Asset whose machine this claim binds.

fields.name: name
fields.description: The name of the object.

fields.name: labels
fields.description: Labels are copied onto the bound Host and removed when the claim goes away, for example role: worker. EndpointProfiles and firmware plans select machines by them. Keys have no prefix (no "/"), so they never clash with the labels the operator sets under metal.pk.io/.

validations.message: label keys must be unprefixed valid label names

fields.name: os
fields.description: OS names the TalosNode the machine should run. Setting it proposes an install that erases the disk chosen by the TalosNode's installDiskSelector. Without it the claim only reserves the machine and nothing is done to it.

validations.message: os.nodeRef is immutable: drop the OS intent first, or create another claim

fields.name: nodeRef
fields.description: NodeRef names the TalosNode (os.pk.io) whose config the machine boots.

fields.name: name
fields.description: The name of the object.

fields.name: provisioning
fields.description: Provisioning tunes how the operator installs the OS onto the machine.

fields.name: approval
fields.description: Approval: Required (default) or Automatic.

fields.name: systemRef
fields.description: SystemRef picks one machine by its Redfish system id when the BMC manages more than one (a multi-node chassis). Leave it out when the BMC manages one machine.

fields.name: name
fields.description: The name of the object.

fields.name: status
fields.description: HostClaimStatus says which machine the claim holds and how far its install got. The Host's spec.claimRef is what actually holds the machine; the first claim to set it wins.

fields.name: blockedOn
fields.description: BlockedOn says why the claim does not continue. Before the bind, it tells why the claim cannot bind (AssetNotFound, AssetNotMaterialized, HostAlreadyClaimed). After the bind, it tells why the install waits (Approval(Provisioning), HeldByUser, HostInMaintenance, OperationFailed). kubectl describe shows the message with the command to run.

fields.name: conditions
fields.description: Conditions are the truth — the only thing reconcilers branch on.

fields.name: lastTransitionTime
fields.description: The time of the last change of the status.

fields.name: message
fields.description: A message for people about the last change. It can be empty.

fields.name: observedGeneration
fields.description: The generation of the object that the condition is for. A lower value than metadata.generation shows an old condition.

fields.name: reason
fields.description: A word in CamelCase that tells why the condition has its status.

fields.name: status
fields.description: The status of the condition: True, False or Unknown.

fields.name: type
fields.description: The type of the condition.

fields.name: handOff
fields.description: HandOff records that the machine was installed: which host runs which TalosNode, from which config, since when. The operator writes it one time, when the boot finishes. This record tells the operator that the work is done. A node that is down later is not installed again. A deletion of old HostOperations changes nothing. It goes away with the claim.

fields.name: at
fields.description: At is when the operator saw the hand-off.

fields.name: configDigest
fields.description: ConfigDigest is sha256:<hex> of the rendered config the machine booted with; empty when the record was rebuilt from an operation that did not carry it.

fields.name: host
fields.description: Host is the Host the node was installed on.

fields.name: node
fields.description: Node is the TalosNode the machine runs.

fields.name: operation
fields.description: Operation is the boot operation (namespace/name) that installed the machine. Empty when the machine already ran the node when the claim found it: the operator never touched it, so a release leaves its power alone.

fields.name: hostRef
fields.description: HostRef names the bound Host.

fields.name: name
fields.description: The name of the object.

fields.name: phase
fields.description: Phase summarizes the conditions below for people and for kubectl columns. It is a summary, not the contract: automation should read conditions.
